newsitem.title: KENYA: More arson attacks around Kenya port of Mombasa.
newsitem.headline: More arson attacks around Kenya port of Mombasa.

text.p: Arsonists razed about 100 roadside kiosks and dozens of houses around Mombasa on Sunday after five Kenyans were killed and many hurt overnight by unidentified attackers, witnesses said.
The government sent in the army to back police and paramilitary units battling to end five days of violence in the area, having withdrawn the soldiers a day earlier.

President Daniel arap Moi, in remarks on state radio, implicated the opposition in the Mombasa violence, saying tribalism had become rampant in the East African country and was being used by "leaders with selfish interests".

Moi, 73 and in power 19 years, said the opposition, battling him for constitutional reforms before elections due later this year, spent all their time talking without contributing to the development of the people.

But in Mombasa, opposition member of parliament Rashid Mzee told the British Broadcasting Corporation he suspected Moi's ruling Kenya African National Union (KANU) party was behind the chaos, as part of a move designed to forestall a campaign for reforms and delay the elections.
Mzee said police had arrested some opposition activists, Moslem leaders and human rights officials in Mombasa.
Several thousand foreign tourists on the coast north and south of Mombasa were advised to stay inside their hotels but no visitors had been caught up in the violence, officials said.
Police figures showed a total of 31 people had been killed in the fighting since it erupted last Wednesday night with an attack on a police station.
Coast province police chief Francis Gichuki told reporters up to 69 people had been arrested and would appear in court on Monday. Three stolen rifles and five pistols had been seized.

"We are treating this as thuggery and do not see a political motive. The situation is fluid but it is under control. It took us by surprise," Gichuki said. The army was on routine exercises in the area and police were using army aircraft to contain the chaos, he said.
The police chief also said two local administrative police had gone missing, but gave no details.
Local residents said those killed were mainly people who originally came from outside the coastal region.
They pointed to leaflets hand-written in Swahili and distributed around the region.
"The time has come for us original inhabitants of the coast to claim what is rightly ours. We must remove these invaders from our land," the pamphlets said.

Reuters reporter Edmund Kwena said a petrol station was attacked and a pump set on fire and he saw scores of buildings torched on Sunday: "I personally counted up to 100 kiosks completely burned down. Dozens of houses were also set on fire in the Diani area, a popular tourist area south of Mombasa."
Kenya's roadside kiosks mostly sell clothing, fresh fruit, vegetables, and handicrafts for tourists.
Truckloads of army troops were immediately deployed in the area and senior army officers arrived by helicopter.

A man was shot by police and his body burned by villagers at Bombolulu, north of Mombasa, on Sunday. The shooting took place after survivors of overnight attacks in neighbouring Shauri Yako slum area accused Bombolulu residents of responsibility.
Residents said dozens of houses in the Maweni and Kongowea areas north of Mombasa were burned on Sunday.
Karl-Heinz Straus, chairman of the Coastal Kenya Association of Tour Operators, said he was worried that chaos could adversely affect tourism.
The industry brought in around $465 million last year from 770,000 visitors -- over half of them people who visited beaches in the Mombasa area.
"The violence is being reported abroad and overseas operators are already making enquiries," said Straus. "Most tourists come to Mombasa and they just won't come when there is violence."
